summary:
MARSCOPE is a layered Mars map for planning a Marswalk. It runs in a phone browser.

What it does: It combines three kinds of NASA data from four missions: optical (Viking, MRO CTX 5 m), thermal (Mars Odyssey THEMIS) and topographic (MGS MOLA). The user taps two points, a science target or a NASA landing site. MARSCOPE shows the distance on Mars, screens the route against canyons, volcano slopes, deep basins and polar ice (LOW, MODERATE or HIGH), suggests a safer detour and lists the nearest NASA landing sites. For routes under 50 km it estimates round-trip walking time against an assumed EVA window and opens CTX imagery so the crew can look for rocks, slopes and dunes.

Example: a 3,204 km route through Valles Marineris is rated HIGH; the detour cuts hazard-zone exposure from 44% to 7% for 13% more distance. A 5.5 km walk takes 3.6 h round trip, 46% of an assumed 8 h EVA window.

Why it matters: Mars Trek shows regional views; MARSCOPE links its layers to a crew's route question, down to 5 m scale, with safety first.

Built with: HTML, JavaScript, Leaflet, NASA Mars Trek tiles, GitHub Pages; made on an iPhone.

Limits: hazard zones are approximate regional boxes; walking speed and EVA window are assumed; rocks are not detected automatically. Radiation data and surface images are future work.

AI use: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code and text at our direction. We chose the challenge, data and features, and tested the app.
details:
MARSCOPE is a layered Mars map for planning a Marswalk. It runs in any phone browser and needs no installation.

What it does: The map combines three kinds of NASA data from four missions: optical (Viking color imagery and MRO CTX 5 m imagery), thermal (Mars Odyssey THEMIS infrared) and topographic (Mars Global Surveyor MOLA elevation). The user switches layers, then taps two points, a science target or a NASA landing site. MARSCOPE shows the route distance on Mars, screens the route against canyons, volcano slopes, deep basins and polar ice with a LOW, MODERATE or HIGH rating, suggests a safer detour, and lists the nearest NASA landing sites. For routes under 50 km it gives a Marswalk estimate (round-trip time at an assumed 3 km/h compared with an assumed 8 h EVA window) and opens CTX imagery in one tap so the crew can look for large rocks, slopes and dunes.

Example mission scenario: A crew lands near a site NASA has already explored, such as Jezero Crater, where Perseverance studies an ancient river delta for signs of past life. The crew taps its landing point and a science target a few kilometers away. MARSCOPE shows the distance, the estimated walking time against the EVA window and the nearest landing sites. The crew then checks CTX imagery for obstacles, with THEMIS and MOLA as extra context.

Example results: A 3,204 km route through Valles Marineris is rated HIGH (45% of the route inside the canyon zone). The suggested detour cuts hazard-zone exposure from 44% to 7% for 13% more distance. A 5.5 km walk shows a 3.6 h round trip, 46% of the assumed EVA window.

Why it matters: Tools such as Mars Trek are built for regional and global views. MARSCOPE links those layers to a simple route question a crew would ask and zooms down to the 5 m scale. Safety comes first: zones warn the crew before they commit to a route.

How it is built: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the open-source Leaflet library, NASA Mars Trek tile services and GitHub Pages hosting. It was built and tested on an iPhone and costs nothing to run.

What is creative: a one-tap workflow from two points to a route briefing, and a detour search that minimizes distance multiplied by a hazard penalty.

Factors we considered: astronaut safety, use on a phone, free and open NASA data, and honesty about approximations.

Limits: Hazard zones are approximate regional boxes, not slope measurements. Walking speed, EVA window and landing site positions are approximate or assumed. Large rocks and local obstacles are not detected automatically; the crew checks them in CTX imagery. Radiation data and surface point-of-view images are planned for future versions.

Use of AI: Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, was used to debug the code and to draft the English text. Our team chose the challenge, data layers and features,did the demo presentation,tested the app on an iPhone and made the decisions. No AI-generated images, audio or video were used, and no NASA logos or branding.
